Voice for the Voiceless

One federation. Ten fronts. One community that no longer waits to be seen.

Since the years that followed the Mandal Commission's 1990 decision to open 27% reservation to India's Other Backward Classes, this Federation has done the unglamorous work of turning a policy on paper into a form filled, a scholarship claimed, a grievance heard. We are not here to speak about backward-class communities. We are that community, organised — from the taluk office to the national stage.

Become a Member See What We've Done
What We Stand For

Backward-class life in India isn't one problem. We stopped pretending it was.

Ask ten different families in ten different districts what's standing in their way, and you'll get ten different answers — a scholarship form nobody explained, a job that needed a skill nobody taught, a clinic that's an hour and a bus fare away. So the Federation works ten fronts at once: Education, Economic Development, Employment, Social Equality, Political Representation, Health, Political Awareness, Digital Inclusion, Women's Empowerment, and Minority & Social Welfare.

01

Education

Scholarship forms are free to apply for and impossible to navigate alone. We sit with families through the paperwork, not just the awareness campaign.

03

Employment

A skill without a placement route is a certificate on a wall. We work the connection between the two.

06

Health

Camps that come to the taluk, not the other way around — because the nearest quality clinic is often the real barrier, not the willingness to go.

About the Federation

We didn't start as an organisation. We started as neighbours explaining a form to each other.

Our Story

In 1990, when the Government of India moved to extend 27% reservation to Other Backward Classes in central services and public sector undertakings, it changed what was legally owed to millions of families overnight — and changed almost nothing about whether those families knew it, or knew how to claim it. That gap, between a right on paper and a right in hand, is where this Federation began: taluk by taluk, with people who understood both the form and the family filling it out.

Karnataka had already lived a version of this story once before. In 1977, under Chief Minister Devaraj Urs, the state stood up its own Backward Classes Welfare Department — one of the earliest institutional acknowledgements anywhere in India that backward-class welfare needed a permanent home, not a one-time gesture. The Federation carries that lineage forward at the community level: where the department is the government's structure, we are the community's own.

What grew from that is now a federated network of taluk, district and state units, coordinated from offices in Bengaluru and New Delhi, organised into a Youth Wing and a Women's Wing, and led by office bearers appointed from within the community they represent. Registered as a society in 1994, with founding units first taking shape in and around Bengaluru — placeholder milestone shown for layout; the Federation's own registration year and founding names should replace this line.

Mission

To unite India's Other Backward Classes under one national platform — advancing education, economic opportunity, employment, social equality, political representation, healthcare access, political awareness, digital inclusion, women's empowerment, and social welfare, while preserving the values and contributions of OBC communities to Indian society.

Vision

A future in which every OBC community, in every state and district, is connected, informed, and equipped with the opportunity, representation, and leadership capacity to participate fully in India's social, economic, and political life — with one united national voice.

Our Roots

We come from the fields, the workshops, and the trades that built this country's economy long before anyone gave them a policy category: weavers, potters, blacksmiths, farmers, and a hundred other hereditary crafts and occupations that Other Backward Classes have carried for generations. The Federation exists to make sure that history is remembered as a source of strength, not treated as a reason for exclusion.

Our Objectives — the founding charter

  • District & state programmesOrganising educational, cultural and social development programmes for backward classes at the taluk, district and state level.
  • Grievance redressalCarrying community grievances to the concerned government officers, and staying with the case until members receive the assistance they're due.
  • Equality & harmonyBuilding equality, brotherhood, co-existence and goodwill among backward-class communities.
  • Education for the poorProgrammes for the education of children from low-income backward-class households.
  • Savings & insurance awarenessEncouraging small savings and building awareness of insurance among members.
  • Reading rooms & vocational trainingFree reading rooms and libraries, and vocational training for unemployed youth, women and people with disabilities.
  • Health campsFree health check-ups, eye tests and blood donation camps, run with local hospitals and health authorities.
  • Documentation supportAssistance with ID, ration card, Aadhaar and revenue-tax matters.
  • Government scheme accessGuiding members through pension, BPL, health insurance and other welfare schemes.
  • Culture, sport & festivalStage, music and sporting programmes, and the celebration of national and state festivals, including Ambedkar Jayanthi.

Meet the people carrying this charter forward →

What We Do

Ten fronts. One federation working all of them at once.

01

Education

Scholarships go unclaimed not because families don't qualify, but because the process was never explained. We run scholarship navigation support, partner with coaching and ed-tech providers, and hold community-level awareness drives before deadlines, not after.

02

Economic Development

Government financial schemes exist; awareness of them often doesn't. We run financial literacy programmes, structured campaigns on welfare schemes, and seed-support networks for first-time entrepreneurs.

03

Employment

Skill without a placement route is a certificate on a wall. We build skilling partnerships, run job-fair and placement drives, and guide members through public-sector employment pathways.

04

Social Equality

Constitutional safeguards exist on paper; discrimination still happens in practice. We document cases, build escalation channels, and run visible community-representation initiatives.

05

Political Representation

Backward-class communities are undercounted in the rooms where policy is actually made. We build leadership pipelines and structured engagement with elected representatives.

06

Health

The nearest quality clinic is often the real barrier, not the willingness to seek care. We run health camps, build insurance-scheme awareness, and partner with public health programmes.

07

Political Awareness

Rights are only useful if people know they hold them. We run civic-education workshops, produce rights-literacy material, and build leadership-development tracks for youth.

08

Digital Inclusion

Government has moved online faster than access and literacy have kept up. We run digital literacy drives and assisted e-governance access points.

09

Women's Empowerment

Economic independence and leadership representation both start with access most women were never given. Our Women's Wing sets real leadership representation targets.

10

Minority & Social Welfare

Welfare schemes exist unevenly, and implementation gaps hit families with the least room to absorb delay. We track scheme implementation and coordinate directly with welfare bodies.

A Wing of the Federation

The doors our founders fought open still take work to walk through. This is who does that work now.

The Youth Wing exists because a right won on paper in 1990 still has to be claimed, generation after generation. Its members run exam and career guidance sessions for peers navigating scholarships, admissions and government job applications; organise sport and cultural programmes that keep young people connected to their district unit; and serve as the Federation's leadership pipeline — the same route through which today's office bearers once started.

A Wing of the Federation

Built by the women it serves — not spoken for on their behalf.

The Women's Wing exists to make sure the Federation's welfare work reaches women directly, not only through the household. Its coordinators run vocational training aimed at making women self-dependent, help members access the women's welfare fund, widow pension and other schemes built specifically for them, and organise health camps and savings-and-insurance awareness sessions grounded in the real budgeting realities of member households.

1

Vocational training

Welfare-fund access

3

Health & wellbeing

Health check-up camps with a focus on women's and children's health.

4

Savings awareness

Sessions on small savings and insurance, built around household budgeting realities.

Open to women members and eligible family members of registered households.

Where This Movement Comes From

Reservation didn't begin in 1990. It began in 1882 — and Karnataka was where it first became policy.

Adapted from the Federation's own "Reservation and Concept of Other Backward Classes" briefing, written by founder J. Enjeerappa. This is the century-and-a-half arc from the first colonial-era proposal to today's reservation arithmetic.

Pre-Independence

The idea of reservation grew directly out of the caste hierarchy itself. British officer Sir William Hunter and social reformer Jyotiba Phule first raised the concept in 1882, pointing to the inequality baked into the caste system. In 1902, Shahu Maharaja, the King of Kolhapur, acted on that idea and implemented 50% reservation in government jobs for backward classes in his state — a move that drew opposition from some quarters even then.

The Kingdom of Mysore took a more deliberate route. In 1918, Maharaja Nalvadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar responded to demands from backward communities by forming a committee under Sir Leslie Miller, then Chief Justice of the Mysore Court, to study social, educational and economic conditions and report back. The Miller Committee delivered its findings in 1919: backward classes should receive reservation in government service, rising to 50% within seven years. Wodeyar implemented these policies in 1921, extending reservation to Lingayats, Vokkaligas, Dalits, Kurubas, Madiwalas, Savita, Uppara, Beda, Besta, Golla, Rajput and other backward castes — a model that, this Federation argues, the rest of the country would take decades to catch up to.

After Independence

Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, as Law Minister, brought the Hindu Code Bill before Parliament in favour of women from backward castes — Vokkaliga, Lingayat, Kuruba, Maratha, Madiwala, Savita, Besta, Beda, Uppara, Kumbara, Vishwakarma and others. When Nehru's government did not carry it through, Ambedkar resigned from the Law Ministry, having also called for a Permanent Commission for the Backward Classes. Reservation frameworks took shape unevenly across the former princely states and presidencies — the Justice Party's caste-based representation in Madras, rules in the Bombay Presidency from 1931, and reservation under the Maharajas of Travancore and Cochin, influenced by Sri Narayana Guru — until the Constitution superseded them all in 1950, embedding backward-class provisions in Articles 15(4) and 16(4). Early court challenges saw these clauses struck down before Ambedkar's first constitutional amendment, in 1951, restored relief for backward castes.

In 1979, Prime Minister Morarji Desai, acting on Chaudhary Charan Singh's advice, set up a commission under B.P. Mandal to identify backward classes nationally and recommend how to lift them up — not on caste grounds alone, but as a matter of social, educational and economic condition. Mandal's report found that OBCs made up 52% of India's population (a 1980 SEBC Commission estimate later cited alongside a separate 58% figure in the Federation's own account) and identified more than 3,700 castes and communities across the country. The Morarji Desai government fell before it could act, and the Congress government that followed did not take the report up. It was Prime Minister V.P. Singh who implemented the Mandal Report in 1990, triggering nationwide protests in which the Federation's records note roughly 62 people died by suicide. The matter reached the Supreme Court, which in 1992 upheld implementation — while capping total reservation at 50% and excluding it from the country's most senior posts.

The Constitution gained a further layer in 2018–19: the 102nd Amendment Act (enacted 11 August 2018) gave the National Commission for Backward Classes constitutional status, and in 2019 the central government added a 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections, with an income ceiling. Reservation in India today stands at SC 15%, ST 7.5%, OBC 27%, and EWS 10% — a combined 59.5%. In Karnataka specifically, the Chinnappa Reddy Commission, implemented in 1990, continues to govern reservation in the state.

"If you want justice for the voiceless, learn to fight, learn to fight step by step. If you want to live, learn to die. Learn to move forward using education as a weapon." — Bharat Ratna Karpoori Thakur, Pioneer of Socialism. Quoted in the Federation's own reservation history document, alongside a companion line from M.K. Gandhi's 17 January 1931 letter from Yerwada Central Jail: "It is believed that great men are responsible for the revolutions that have taken place in this world. In reality, it is the people who are responsible for it."

Civic Education

Know Your Constitution — the rights and safeguards behind our work.

The Constitution is a vast document, but the idea at its core is simple, and it belongs to every citizen. This is a short, plain-language guide to the parts of it our members ask about most — adapted from "Namma Samvidhana" (Our Constitution, In Brief), the Kannada civic pamphlet by Mangalore Vijaya, translated here for wider reach.

2y 11mThe Constituent Assembly sat for 2 years, 11 months and 18 days, across 11 sessions and 166 sitting days — 114 of them spent on the draft alone.
Nov 26, 1949The date the Assembly finally adopted the Constitution, after more than two thousand amendments and suggestions were discussed.
Jan 26, 1950The date it came into force — the day India became a sovereign, democratic republic under its own free Constitution.

Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, appointed Chairman of the Drafting Committee on 29 August 1947, is remembered as the chief architect of the document — a role that fell to him almost single-handedly after other members of the Committee resigned, fell ill, or were occupied with state affairs, and which he is recorded as having carried out with exhausting effort and great care. Karnataka's own representatives sat on that Constituent Assembly too, among them C.M. Poonacha, K.C. Reddy, T. Siddalingaiah, K. Hanumanthaiah and others from the Mysore and Coorg provinces.

Fundamental Rights — Part III

The rights every citizen can enforce in a court of law.

Article 14

Equality Before Law

The State cannot deny any person equality before the law or equal protection of the laws.

Article 15

No Discrimination

No citizen may be discriminated against on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth — while the State keeps the power to make special provisions for women, children, and socially and educationally backward classes.

Article 16

Equal Public Employment

Equal opportunity in State employment for all, with the State empowered to reserve posts for classes it finds inadequately represented, including in promotions for SCs and STs.

Article 17

Abolition of Untouchability

Untouchability is abolished in every form, and enforcing any disability arising from it is a punishable offence.

Article 19

Freedoms

Speech and expression, peaceful assembly, forming associations, moving and settling freely, and practising any profession or trade.

Article 21 & 21A

Life, Liberty & Education

No person may be deprived of life or liberty except by lawful procedure; every child aged 6–14 has a right to free, compulsory education.

Article 23 & 24

No Forced Labour or Child Labour

Trafficking and begar are prohibited; no child under 14 may work in a factory, mine, or hazardous job.

Article 25 & 26

Freedom of Religion

Freedom of conscience and to profess, practise and propagate religion, and for religious denominations to manage their own institutions.

Article 29 & 30

Minority Rights

The right to conserve a distinct language, script or culture, and for minorities to establish and run their own educational institutions.

Directive Principles — Part IV

Not enforceable in court, but stated as fundamental to how the country is governed.

Article 38 & 39

A Just Social Order

The State works to minimise inequality in income, status and opportunity, secure a livelihood for all, and prevent wealth from concentrating in a few hands.

Article 39A

Free Legal Aid

Equal opportunity for justice, including free legal aid so no citizen is shut out by poverty or disability.

Article 40

Village Panchayats

The State organises panchayats and gives them the powers to function as real units of self-government.

Article 41–43

Work & Living Wage

Provision for work, education and public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age or sickness, and a living wage with humane working conditions.

Article 45

Early Childhood Care

Care and education for every child until age six.

Article 46 & 47

Weaker Sections & Public Health

Special care for the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and other weaker sections, and a duty to raise nutrition and public health standards.

Fundamental Duties — Part IVA, Article 51A

  1. Abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals, the Flag and the Anthem.
  2. Cherish the ideals that inspired the freedom struggle.
  3. Uphold the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.
  4. Defend the country and render national service when called upon.
  5. Promote harmony and common brotherhood across religion, language, region and section, and renounce practices derogatory to women's dignity.
  1. Value and preserve our composite culture.
  2. Protect the environment and have compassion for living creatures.
  3. Develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry.
  4. Safeguard public property and abjure violence.
  5. Strive for excellence in every sphere, individual and collective.
  6. As a parent or guardian, provide education to your child between ages six and fourteen.

Where "Backward Classes" appears in the Constitution

The specific provisions this Federation's advocacy rests on — the constitutional basis for reservation and representation.

Article 15(4) & 16(4)
Empower the State to make special provisions and reserve appointments for socially and educationally backward classes, and for SCs and STs.
Article 46
Directs the State to promote, with special care, the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections and protect them from social injustice.
Article 243D & 243T
Reserve seats and Chairperson offices for SCs, STs and women in Panchayats and Municipalities, and allow states to reserve further seats for backward classes.
Article 330 & 332
Reserve seats for SCs and STs in the Lok Sabha and in every State Legislative Assembly, in proportion to their population.
Article 334
Sets the sunset clause on that reservation — most recently extended by the 126th Amendment, passed in December 2019, through to 2030.
Article 338 & 338A
Establish the National Commissions for Scheduled Castes and for Scheduled Tribes, with powers to investigate complaints and advise on policy.
Article 340
Empowers the President to appoint a Commission to investigate the conditions of socially and educationally backward classes and recommend steps to improve them — the constitutional root of the OBC classification this Federation was built around.
Articles 341 & 342
Set out how castes, races or tribes are notified as Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes for constitutional purposes.

Adapted from "Namma Samvidhana (Ati Sankshiptadalli)" — Our Constitution, In Brief — a Kannada civic pamphlet by Mangalore Vijaya, presented here in English. Content is simplified for a general audience and is not a substitute for legal advice; please verify specific provisions against the official text before relying on them.

In Print

People's Document — the Federation's own monthly, in the voices of the people it's written for.

Launched in May 2025 as an "Empowerment Journal for Deprived Classes," People's Document is published by Manimozhi Pathipakam and carries expert-driven articles, interviews and case studies on the realities facing OBC, MBC, SC and ST communities — for private circulation, published with the support of patrons, with every article released under the full responsibility of its author.

From the Editor's Note

"A document is memory, proof, and perspective. It is a tool for change when truth is told boldly," writes Editor K. Subramanian in the inaugural issue. The editorial asks why a nation whose majority are Backward, Most Backward, Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe citizens still sees roughly 17% of the population dominate the state apparatus, the highest administrative posts and the judiciary — and commits the magazine to standing "where such truths are written without fear and read with purpose."

Exclusive: Mr. Srinivasachary, IAS

The inaugural issue's featured interview is with the retired State Election Commissioner of Karnataka, who argues that OBC demands are not favours but constitutional rights: "A unified and strategic approach is essential to eliminate disparities, secure equitable opportunities, and achieve true social justice for OBCs and other deprived classes." Belonging to a Most Backward Class community himself, he traces the struggle back through school-day social boycotts to a thousand years of caste discrimination that predates the "Depressed Classes" label.

From the Founder's Interview: why 56%?

People's Document's interview with Federation founder J. Enjeerappa — conducted through Uvarman, the bi-monthly published by Thiruvannamalai Manimozhi Publications — traces his own path from leading the Madivala Youth Association (2002–2004) through the presidency of the All India Dhobi Mahasabha (2017–2019) to founding the OBC Federation of India. He led a 48-day Rath Yatra from Kanyakumari to Delhi, rerouted through Karnataka during the Jallikattu protests, to press the demand that the Dhobi (laundry-worker) community — already classified as Scheduled Caste in 18 states and six Union Territories — receive the same recognition in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

His central argument in the interview: if government statistics put the OBC population at 56% of the nation, reservation should reflect that proportion, not remain capped at the Mandal Commission's 27%. "We firmly believe that if all backward communities unite and raise their voices collectively, we can bring about a significant transformation in our country," he told the magazine, while acknowledging that leaders across the political spectrum — including Union Home Minister Amit Shah, Bihar CM Nitish Kumar, former CM Lalu Prasad Yadav, and Karnataka's Governor and Chief Minister — have "listened with interest and empathy," with "no substantive follow-up action" so far.
